newsitem.title: USA: Presidential debates a tale of gaffes and glory.
newsitem.headline: Presidential debates a tale of gaffes and glory.

text.p: John Kennedy rolls his eyes in mock alarm as Richard Nixon speaks. Ronald Reagan laughs off a Jimmy Carter remark. George Bush sneaks a look at his watch.

This is all on tape, vivid moments from U.S. presidential campaign debates, and Texas billionaire Ross Perot tried recently to explain what these televised talkfests mean to someone who wants to be president of the United States.
"We can't possibly win if we're not in those debates," said Perot, a third-party nominee suing to stop President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole from excluding him this year.
Clinton and Dole have agreed to meet one-on-one on Sunday in Hartford, Connecticut, and on October 16 in San Diego, California.
"We've got to get in the game and we will," said Perot.

A judge rejected his suit and he has only a faint hope of winning on appeal, but count on Perot to put things bluntly: In modern White House campaigns, debates have indeed been a key to "the game" -- and have sometimes been the game itself, crucial to the election.

It makes no difference that they have never been real debates in any classic sense since Kennedy and Nixon began the modern-day showdowns in 1960. It makes no difference that theatrics notoriously overshadow substance almost every time.
Nor does it matter that the debates have probably not had a decisive impact on the election outcome since Reagan one-upped Carter repeatedly in the lone 1980 campaign debate.
They attract huge TV audiences, they give underdogs a matchless chance to turn things around, they make favourites face the cold-sweat risk of saying something stupid.

And if Dole does upset Clinton on Nov. 5, the morning-after analysts will surely echo Carter's view after his narrow win over then-President Gerald Ford in 1976: "If it hadn't been for the debates, I would have lost."

Television has moved on from small-screen black-and-white and the audience has grown by tens of millions since the prototype Kennedy-Nixon debates of 1960. but the stakes and standards were pretty much set by those encounters.

Kennedy, a Massachusetts Senator fighting anti-Catholic prejudice, and Nixon, Dwight Eisenhower's vice president, had four debates. But it was the first one, in Chicago, that enabled Kennedy to shatter Nixon's aura of superiority.
He ignored his rival to address lofty themes to the TV audience. "It's time America started moving again," he said.
Nixon addressed Kennedy, following classic narrow rules of debate, replying to specific points on specific issues.
That was a mistake, and it was compounded by what TV did to a man who perspired easily, was haggard from illness, had a five o'clock shadow and shunned effective makeup.
Kennedy looked cool, and as Nixon spoke he would often fix him with a sidewise stare that suggested disbelief, amusement or alarm depending on the height of Kennedy's eyebrow.
The cameras feasted on it and so did the audience. Polls showed that TV viewers rated Kennedy the winner by 2-1, while those who listened on radio thought the contest even.
Six percent of viewers said the debates decided them. Three quarters, or about three million, voted for Kennedy. He won by 112,000 votes and gave credit where he thought it was due.
"It was TV more than anything else," he said.

No more presidential debates occurred for 16 years -- they have been a fixture of every campaign since -- when the 1976 Ford-Carter clash established a cardinal rule: even a single verbal gaffe can be fatal, if it is bad enough.
They met three times, but what remains are a few stunning words uttered by Ford in Round Two: "There is no Soviet domination of Eastern Europe."
A furore erupted. A comeback Ford had been making in the polls deflated. Democrat Carter eked out a win on voting day.
He then risked all on one 1980 debate with Reagan and set people to giggling by suggesting he consulted daughter Amy on world affairs. Worse, Reagan caught him flat-footed, twice.
He accused Carter of distorting his record and gleefully topped him with a much-quoted quip, "There you go again."
And he crystalized national discontent with economic conditions in one biting question to viewers: "Are you and your family better off than you were four years ago?"

No succeeding campaign debate has matched the impact of those early encounters. Walter Mondale, Michael Dukakis and Bush went into the debates of 1984, '88 and '92 far behind in the polls and did nothing to improve their prospects.

The most vivid moment of the three-way Bush-Clinton-Perot contests of 1992 may have been visual rather than verbal: Bush glancing furtively at his watch while the others talked, the very image of a man for whom time was running out.
Negative impressions like that can be enduring, and no one knows it better than Dole as he prepares for the 1996 round.

In 1976, as Ford's running mate, he came on like a truculent attack-dog in a vice-presidential debate with Mondale, including a bitter reference to World War II -- in which he suffered crippling wounds -- as "a Democrat war."
That established his reputation as a caustic gut-fighter, a one-dimensional and unfair image he has been trying to soften ever since. He gets his last best chance on Sunday.
